heading: Velocity and distance
text: Differentiation recovers velocity from a distance function, while integration recovers the change in distance from velocity. Geometrically, velocity is the slope of the distance graph and change in distance is signed area under the velocity graph.
formulas: change in f = signed area under v

heading: Constant velocity
text: For constant velocity, distance is a linear function of time. The initial distance changes the intercept but not the slope.

heading: Forward and backward motion
text: If a car moves forward at velocity V for time T and then backward at velocity -V for the same time, its final displacement is zero. The positive and negative rectangular areas under the velocity graph cancel.

heading: Functions, domain, and range
text: A function assigns one output to each input in its domain. The domain is the allowed set of inputs and the range is the set of resulting outputs. A distance function can be continuous while its velocity changes by jumps.

heading: Slope in a break-even model
text: For a linear cost and linear income model, break-even occurs where the two functions are equal. Comparing their slopes determines whether income can eventually catch cost.

heading: Differences and sums
text: For values sampled at equally spaced times, a discrete velocity is the difference between consecutive distances. Adding all consecutive differences recovers the total change in distance because the intermediate terms cancel.

heading: Piecewise linear calculus
text: On each linear segment, velocity is the constant slope of the distance graph. Conversely, the signed area under a piecewise constant velocity graph gives the change in distance over the interval.

heading: Composition multiplies slopes
text: For the linear functions g(t) = 2t + 1 and f(t) = 4t, composing f after g gives f(g(t)) = 8t + 4. Its slope 8 is the product of the slopes 4 and 2.

heading: Step functions and concentrated change
text: A short burst of large velocity can produce a fixed change in distance. As the burst becomes narrower and taller while its area stays fixed, the distance approaches a step and the velocity approaches an impulse-like delta function.

heading: Recovering distance from two constant speeds
text: If velocity is 2 until t = 5 and 3 afterward, with f(0) = 0, continuity fixes the second linear piece. At t = 5 the distance is 10, so afterward f(t) = 10 + 3(t - 5).

heading: Average velocity
text: Average velocity over an interval is change in distance divided by change in time. On the graph of distance, it is the slope of the secant line joining the two endpoints.

heading: Instantaneous velocity
text: Instantaneous velocity is the limiting value of average velocity as the time interval shrinks to zero. Geometrically, secant lines approach the tangent line and their slopes approach the derivative.

heading: Velocity for f(t) = t^2
text: For f(t) = t^2, the average velocity from t to t + h simplifies to 2t + h. Letting h approach zero gives the instantaneous velocity v(t) = 2t.

heading: Constant acceleration
text: Under constant acceleration a, velocity is linear and distance is quadratic. The constant b is initial velocity and c is initial distance.

heading: Local slope and accumulated area
text: Slope is local: velocity at one instant depends on the distance graph near that instant. Accumulated distance is global: finding area up to a time requires the earlier velocity history and an initial distance.
formulas: v(t) depends on f near t
f(t) = f(0) + accumulated area under v
